tips.title: State hoisting keeps composables stateless, reusable, and testable
tips.content:
A composable that owns its own mutable state internally (via remember)
can only be controlled from inside itself — the caller can't observe,
override, or drive that state from outside, which limits reuse and makes
unit testing the composable's behavior harder.

Hoisting state means the composable accepts the current value and an
onValueChange callback as parameters instead of holding state internally
— the caller owns the state, and the composable becomes a pure function
of its inputs, which is both more reusable and trivially testable.

tips.title: @Stable and @Immutable let Compose skip recomposition for unchanged data
tips.content:
Compose's recomposition skipping relies on being able to prove a
composable's inputs haven't meaningfully changed — a class Compose can't
prove is stable (like one with a public var, or a plain interface with no
annotation) forces recomposition on every pass even if nothing actually
changed, since Compose can't safely assume otherwise.

@Immutable promises all properties are truly immutable after
construction; @Stable promises equals() reflects logical equality and
notifies Compose on any change — annotating your own data classes
correctly (or letting the compiler infer stability for simple data
classes with val properties) unlocks proper skipping.

tips.title: LaunchedEffect restarts whenever any of its keys change
tips.content:
LaunchedEffect(key1, key2) { ... } launches a coroutine tied to the
composition, but critically, it cancels and relaunches that coroutine
any time any of the given keys change value between recompositions —
passing the wrong key (or Unit when a real dependency exists) is a common
source of stale-data or missed-update bugs.

Pass Unit only when the effect genuinely should run exactly once for the
composable's lifetime; pass the actual data the effect depends on
otherwise, so the effect correctly restarts when that data changes.

tips.title: DisposableEffect runs cleanup when leaving composition or when keys change
tips.content:
Some side effects need explicit teardown — registering a listener,
subscribing to a system callback — where simply launching a coroutine
isn't the right tool, since there's no suspend-based API to clean up.

DisposableEffect requires an onDispose {} block at the end, which runs
when the composable leaves the composition or when its keys change
before the effect re-runs — forgetting the onDispose block is a compile
error, which prevents accidentally leaking a registered listener.

tips.title: SideEffect publishes Compose state to non-Compose code on every successful recomposition
tips.content:
Sometimes you need to push the current Compose state out to a non-
Compose system (analytics, a legacy View, a third-party SDK) that isn't
aware of Compose's snapshot system — a plain function call during
composition isn't safe, since composition can be re-run or discarded.

SideEffect {} schedules its block to run after every successful (not
discarded) recomposition, guaranteeing it only runs when the composition
actually commits, safely bridging Compose state out to imperative code.

tips.title: CompositionLocal passes implicit values down the tree without threading them through every parameter
tips.content:
Passing a theme, a locale, or a shared configuration object through every
composable's parameter list, layer after layer, adds boilerplate to
every composable in the tree even when most of them never use the value
directly.

CompositionLocalProvider makes a value implicitly available to every
descendant composable without explicit parameter threading — MaterialTheme
itself is built this way, providing colors/typography/shapes implicitly
to every composable under it via LocalContentColor and similar locals.

tips.title: Modifier order changes the resulting layout and behavior, not just its appearance
tips.content:
Modifiers are applied in the exact order they're chained, and each one
wraps the result of the previous one — padding().clickable() gives the
clickable ripple a larger tappable area including the padding, while
clickable().padding() confines the ripple to the original smaller
bounds before padding is applied.

This isn't a stylistic detail — reordering modifiers like size, padding,
clip, and clickable genuinely changes touch target size, ripple bounds,
and clipping behavior, so modifier order should be treated as meaningful
logic, not just a list of properties.

tips.title: key() gives LazyColumn items stable identity across reordering and insertion
tips.content:
Without an explicit key, LazyColumn/LazyRow identify items by their
position in the list — inserting or removing an item near the top shifts
every subsequent item's position, causing Compose to treat items that
didn't actually change as if they did, losing per-item state (scroll
position within an item, animation state) and hurting recomposition
efficiency.

Passing a stable, unique key (typically the item's ID) lets Compose track
each item by identity rather than position, correctly preserving
per-item state and minimizing unnecessary recomposition when the list is
reordered, filtered, or has items inserted.

tips.title: rememberCoroutineScope gives a scope tied to the composition, for launching from callbacks
tips.content:
LaunchedEffect only launches from within composition itself and can't be
called from an event callback like onClick, since callbacks run outside
the composition phase entirely.

rememberCoroutineScope returns a CoroutineScope tied to the composable's
lifecycle (cancelled when it leaves composition) that you can hold onto
and call .launch {} from inside a callback — this is the correct tool
for starting a coroutine in response to a user action, rather than a
composition-driven side effect.

tips.title: Slot APIs let a composable accept flexible content instead of fixed parameters
tips.content:
A composable with a fixed set of parameters (icon: ImageVector, title:
String) can't accommodate every visual variation a caller might need —
adding a badge, a custom icon composable, or a subtitle each requires
modifying the composable's own parameter list.

A slot API accepts one or more @Composable lambda parameters ('slots')
that the caller fills with arbitrary content, giving full layout and
composable freedom without the base composable needing to anticipate
every variation — this is how Scaffold's topBar/bottomBar/content
parameters work.

tips.title: Multiple @Preview annotations render several configurations from one function
tips.content:
Checking how a composable looks in dark mode, at a larger font scale, or
on a tablet-sized screen by manually switching the emulator/device
configuration for each check is slow feedback compared to seeing them all
at once in the IDE.

Stacking multiple @Preview annotations on the same composable (each with
different uiMode, fontScale, or device parameters) renders every variant
side-by-side in Android Studio's preview pane simultaneously, without
needing to run the app at all.

tips.title: produceState bridges a non-Compose async source into Compose State
tips.content:
Adapting a callback-based API (a legacy listener interface, a third-party
SDK) into something a composable can observe directly usually requires
manually wiring a remember { mutableStateOf() } and updating it inside an
effect — produceState packages exactly that pattern into a single,
purpose-built API.

produceState launches a coroutine scoped to the composition and gives you
a State to update as new values arrive, automatically triggering
recomposition on each update — it's the standard bridge for turning any
async data source into something a composable can collect as State.

tips.title: snapshotFlow converts Compose State reads into a cold Flow of changes
tips.content:
Compose's State objects aren't Flows themselves, so reacting to a State
value changing using standard Flow operators (debounce, distinctUntilChanged,
map) isn't directly possible without a bridge.

snapshotFlow { someState.value } creates a Flow that emits a new value
any time the read State object's snapshot changes, letting you apply
normal Flow operators to Compose state — commonly used to debounce a
search query TextField's value before triggering a network call.

tips.title: Unstable lambda captures can defeat recomposition skipping even for otherwise-stable composables
tips.content:
A lambda parameter like onClick: () -> Unit is generally considered
stable by Compose only if it doesn't capture unstable values — a lambda
created inline inside a parent composable that captures a changing local
variable is recreated on every parent recomposition, which can cascade
unnecessary recomposition into the child even if the child's other
parameters didn't change.

Wrapping such a lambda in remember(key) { { ... } }, or restructuring so
the lambda only captures stable values, keeps the same lambda instance
across recompositions where the underlying logic hasn't actually changed.

tips.title: A custom Layout composable gives full control over the measure and placement phases
tips.content:
Standard layouts (Row, Column, Box) cover most needs, but a genuinely
custom arrangement — a circular layout, a staggered grid with specific
sizing rules — sometimes needs direct control over how children are
measured and where they're placed, which no combination of existing
layouts can express.

The Layout composable gives you a measure lambda where you explicitly
measure each child (with constraints you choose) and then place each one
at specific coordinates — this is the same low-level primitive Row,
Column, and Box are themselves built on top of.

tips.title: Semantics modifiers make composables accessible and testable
tips.content:
Compose doesn't automatically know what a custom-drawn composable
represents semantically the way a native Android View's accessibility
node graph might infer from its type — a Canvas-drawn icon or a custom
Composable button has no inherent accessibility description or test
identity unless one is added explicitly.

Modifier.semantics { contentDescription = "..." } provides screen-reader
descriptions, and Modifier.testTag("...") gives a stable identifier for
UI tests (via onNodeWithTag) — both are essential for composables that
don't use a built-in component like Icon or Text that already handles
this.

tips.title: animate*AsState turns a target value change into an automatic, cancellable animation
tips.content:
Manually animating a value change (a color shift, a size change) with a
raw Animatable requires explicitly launching a coroutine and calling
animateTo — more setup than most simple, state-driven animations
actually need.

animateColorAsState, animateDpAsState, animateFloatAsState, and similar
functions take a target value and return a State that automatically
animates toward it whenever the target changes, cancelling and
redirecting any in-flight animation if the target changes again mid-
animation — no manual coroutine management required.
tips.codeSnippet:
val backgroundColor by animateColorAsState(
    targetValue = if (isSelected) Color.Blue else Color.Gray,
    label = "backgroundColor"
)
Box(Modifier.background(backgroundColor)) // animates automatically on state change

tips.title: BoxWithConstraints exposes incoming constraints for responsive, constraint-aware layouts
tips.content:
A composable normally can't see the size constraints it's being measured
within during composition itself — it only receives them during the
separate measure phase, which is invisible to composable logic like `if`
branches choosing between layout variants.

BoxWithConstraints exposes minWidth/maxWidth/minHeight/maxHeight as
values readable inside its content lambda, letting you branch between
entirely different layouts (a compact vs expanded variant) based on the
actual available space, which is the foundation of adaptive/responsive
Compose layouts.

tips.title: AnnotatedString applies multiple styles within a single Text composable
tips.content:
A single Text composable only accepts one uniform style for its entire
content — highlighting part of a sentence in bold, a different color, or
a different size requires either splitting into multiple Text composables
(breaking natural text flow and wrapping) or a different approach
entirely.

AnnotatedString lets you attach SpanStyle ranges to specific character
ranges within one continuous string, so a single Text composable can
render mixed styling — bold, colored, or clickable spans — while text
wrapping and layout still flow naturally as one paragraph.

tips.title: collectAsStateWithLifecycle over collectAsState
tips.content:
collectAsState keeps collecting a Flow even when the app is backgrounded,
wasting resources and potentially causing crashes from state updates on
a torn-down composition.

collectAsStateWithLifecycle stops collection when the lifecycle drops below
STARTED and resumes automatically, matching repeatOnLifecycle semantics —
it's the recommended default for any Flow originating from a ViewModel.

tips.title: Type-safe navigation routes with @Serializable
tips.content:
Navigation Compose 2.8+ supports typed route objects instead of raw string
paths, removing an entire class of bugs from manual argument encoding/decoding.

Pass only primitive IDs through the route and resolve full objects inside the
destination's ViewModel via SavedStateHandle.toRoute<T>() — passing large
objects through navigation arguments bloats the saved state and breaks
process-death restoration.

tips.title: Think in composables, not views
tips.content:
In Compose, UI is built with functions annotated @Composable.
Unlike XML layouts, you describe WHAT the UI should look like,
and the framework figures out HOW to render and update it.

Each composable function is a building block. You compose them together
like Lego pieces — a Screen calls a Header, which calls a Title, etc.

When state changes, only the composables reading that state recompose.
This is fundamentally different from the View system where you manually
find views and update them.

tips.title: remember saves values across recompositions
tips.content:
Composable functions can be called many times (recomposition).
Local variables are reset on every call. Use 'remember' to retain
a value across recompositions.

'remember' stores the value in the composition. It survives
recomposition but NOT configuration changes (like screen rotation).
For that, use 'rememberSaveable'.

Pair remember with mutableStateOf to create observable state
that triggers recomposition when changed.

tips.title: State hoisting for reusable composables
tips.content:
State hoisting moves state UP to the caller, making your composable
stateless and reusable. The composable receives state as parameters
and emits events via callbacks.

Pattern: (value: T, onValueChange: (T) -> Unit)

This makes composables easier to test, preview, and reuse.
The parent decides where the state lives (ViewModel, remember, etc.),
and the child just renders whatever it receives.

tips.title: rememberSaveable survives process death; remember only survives recomposition
tips.content:
remember keeps a value across recompositions but loses it on
configuration changes and process death, since it's just held in memory
tied to the composition instance.

rememberSaveable additionally saves the value into the Activity's saved
state (via the same Bundle mechanism as onSaveInstanceState), so it
survives rotation and process death — use it for UI state that should
persist across those events, like a text field's current input or a
selected tab.
tips.codeSnippet:
var query by remember { mutableStateOf("") } // lost on rotation
var selectedTab by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(0) } // survives rotation and process death
